title: One who sees all beings in the self does not shrink from anything
theme: Seeing all beings in the self and the self in all beings, and the freedom from aversion that follows.

words.role: subject of anupaśyati; picked up by an understood saḥ (‘he’) before vijugupsate
words.context: Śaṅkara: «परिव्राट् मुमुक्षुः», the renunciant who seeks liberation; Deśika: «स इति प्रतिनिर्देशोऽध्याहार्यः», ‘he’ is to be supplied

words.role: marks a contrast with the ‘slayers of the self’ of mantra 3
words.context: Deśika: «ब्रह्मविन्माहात्म्यविशेषद्योतनाय तुशब्दः», ‘tu points to the special greatness of the knower of Brahman’

words.gram: n. acc. pl. (past participle of √भू used as a noun)
words.meaning: beings, things that have come to be
words.context: Śaṅkara: «अव्यक्तादीनि स्थावरान्तानि», ‘from the unmanifest down to the motionless’; Deśika: «ब्रह्मादिस्थावरान्तानि», ‘from Brahmā down to the motionless’

Śaṅkara: «आत्मव्यतिरिक्तानि न पश्यतीत्यर्थः», ‘he sees none apart from the self’

words.context: Deśika: «अनुस्यूतं विशदं निध्यायति», ‘contemplates clearly [the self] as running through [them]’

words.gram: verb, root gup with the suffix san (stem jugups-), present 3rd sg. ātmanepada, with the preverb vi

words.context: Śaṅkara: «विजुगुप्सां घृणां न करोति», ‘does not feel aversion, disgust’; Deśika: ‘blames nothing’; Madhva reads it as ‘wishes to hide himself’

sandhi.rule: A visarga before t becomes s: P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

Final i before an unlike vowel becomes y (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)): bhūtāni ātmani → bhūtāny ātmani, ātmani eva → ātmany eva. Then a + a → ā (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)): eva anupaśyati → evānupaśyati. Advaita Sharada and Deśika’s mūla print भूतानि आत्मन्येव in hiatus as a reading aid.

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (-aḥ before a voiced consonant)
sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o: the visarga goes to u (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)) and a + u gives o (P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः)).

samasa.vigraha: सर्वाणि च तानि भूतानि च सर्वभूतानि, तेषु

morphology.note: The Upaniṣad witnesses read ātmani, the classical locative. The Saṃhitā witnesses (K, M) read ātman, an endingless locative of the Vedic language, and Mahīdhara comments on exactly this: «आत्मन् । सप्तम्या लुक् ।» — ‘ātman: the locative ending is dropped’. Such loss of a case ending in Vedic is covered by P. 7.1.39 (सुपां सुलुक्पूर्वसवर्णाऽऽच्छेयाडाड्यायाजालः), which lists luk among the Vedic substitutes for a case ending. The meaning is the same.

paśyati is the present of dṛś ‘to see’ (the present stem paśya- replaces the root). The preverb anu adds ‘along, after, repeatedly’: to see something as running through everything, or to see it again and again. The pada-pāṭha of VS 40.6 marks it as a preverb compound: «अ॒नु॒पश्य॒तीत्य॑नु॒ऽपश्य॑ति».

Formally a desiderative-shaped stem of gup (‘to guard’), jugups-, used not as a desiderative but with its own meaning ‘to shrink from, despise’. The suffix san after gup in this sense is taught by P. 3.1.5 (गुप्तिज्किद्भ्यः सन्), the same rule Mahīdhara cites for the Mādhyandina reading vi cikitsati (‘doubts’) from kit: «'गुप्तिज्किद्भ्यः सन्' (पा० ३ । १।५) इति स्वार्थे सन्प्रत्ययः». The middle ending -te belongs to the Kāṇva form; the Mādhyandina form cikitsati is active.

The ablative adverb of tad: ‘from that’. Śaṅkara takes it causally (‘from that seeing’); it can also be temporal (‘thereafter’) or refer to the beings (‘from them’). Deśika: «कुतश्चिदपि न विजुगुप्सते», ‘he shrinks from nothing whatever’.

anvaya: यः तु सर्वाणि भूतानि आत्मनि एव अनुपश्यति सर्वभूतेषु च आत्मानम् [अनुपश्यति] [सः] ततः न विजुगुप्सते ।
syntax: A relative-correlative sentence. The relative clause (yas tu … anupaśyati … ātmānam) has one verb, anupaśyati, with two objects joined by ca: ‘all beings in the self’ and ‘the self in all beings’. The main clause, tato na vijugupsate, has no expressed subject: the correlative saḥ (‘he’) is understood, as Deśika notes. tataḥ links the two: the not-shrinking comes from, or after, the seeing.

ambiguities.note: ātman can be one’s own self or the self of all. Śaṅkara reads it as one’s own self, the witness of all cognitions, which is the self of all beings: «अहमेवात्मेति सर्वभूतेषु चात्मानं निर्विशेषं». Deśika reads it as the inner self of all, the Lord: «अत्रात्मशब्दः सङ्कोचकाभावात् प्रकरणादर्थस्वभावाच्च सर्वान्तरात्मविषयः». Madhva, citing a verse, takes it as the Paramātman present in all.

ambiguities.topic: विजुगुप्सते: aversion, blame, hiding or doubt
ambiguities.note: The Kāṇva verb is read as ‘feel aversion or disgust’ (Śaṅkara), ‘blame, censure’ (Deśika: «क्वचिदपि निन्दां न करोतीत्यर्थः») or, from gup ‘to guard’, ‘wish to hide/protect oneself’ (Madhva’s cited verse: «नात्मानं गोप्तुमिच्छति», ‘he does not wish to guard himself’, because there is nothing to fear). The Mādhyandina recension has a different verb, vi cikitsati, ‘doubts’, which Mahīdhara glosses «न संशेते».
A difference of form between the Upaniṣad and Saṃhitā witnesses, not of meaning (see the morphology note and corrections.json).

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, the half-lines have 15 and 16 syllables. The first half-line reaches 16 when the semivowel of bhūtāny ātmany is pronounced as a vowel — bhūtāni ātmani, the hiatus Advaita Sharada prints — a resolution Vedic metre often requires. The edition reports the count and does not alter the text.

translation.literal: But who sees all beings in the self alone, and the self in all beings — [he] from that does not shrink away.
translation.readable: Whoever sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, no longer shrinks from anything.

beginner: Most of our dislike of others begins with a line we draw: here am I, and over there is someone different, strange, perhaps threatening. This verse describes a person for whom that line has faded. Such a person looks at every living thing and finds it held within their own deepest self; and looks into their own self and finds it present in every living thing. The verse then says what follows: that person does not recoil from anyone or anything. Disgust and contempt need distance; there must be an ‘other’ to push away. When the other is seen as part of oneself, the push has nowhere to go. The verse does not tell us to force ourselves to like everyone. It says that a certain way of seeing, once it is real, makes aversion fall away by itself.
analogy: Your left hand does not feel disgust when your right hand is hurt and dirty; it simply reaches over to help, because both belong to one body.

commentary.q: What does the mantra itself say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It describes a person (yas tu, ‘but whoever’) by what that person sees — ‘all beings in the self alone’ and ‘the self in all beings’ — and states one consequence: ‘from that, he does not shrink away’ (tato na vijugupsate). It is a description, not a command; the only verb of seeing is anupaśyati, which carries the sense of seeing along, or again and again. The mantra does not define the self, nor say whether the seeing is a practice or an achievement.

commentary.q: How does Śaṅkara read the two directions of seeing?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For Śaṅkara the seer is a renunciant seeking liberation, and both directions express one knowledge. He sees all beings, from the unmanifest down to the motionless, in the self, and none apart from it («आत्मव्यतिरिक्तानि न पश्यतीत्यर्थः»); and he sees in all beings the same self, his own, the witness of every cognition, without distinction («सर्वभूतेषु चात्मानं निर्विशेषं»). The absence of aversion is not a further command but a description of what follows naturally: «प्राप्तस्यैवानुवादोऽयम्» — ‘this restates what is already the case’. His reason: «सर्वा हि घृणा आत्मनोऽन्यद्दुष्टं पश्यतो भवति» — all disgust arises in one who sees something other than the self as bad; for one who sees only the utterly pure self, there is no other thing to give rise to it.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Deśika continues his reading of mantra 1: everything has Brahman as its self. Here ātman means the inner self of all, the Lord, and the restrictive eva means that the beings, though supported by the elements, rest finally in the Supreme Self («परमात्मन्येव स्थितमित्येवकाराभिप्रायः»). ‘The self in all beings’ only says that he pervades them, for he is not supported by them («व्याप्तिमात्रपरम् । तस्य तैर्धार्यत्वाभावात्»). Because the knower sees everything as the Lord’s own glory, he censures nothing: «क्वचिदपि निन्दां न करोतीत्यर्थः».

commentary.q: What is the shrinking away that ends?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The Kāṇva verb vi-jugupsate is built on gup, ‘to guard’, with a suffix (P. 3.1.5 (गुप्तिज्किद्भ्यः सन्)) that gives it the sense ‘to shrink from, recoil, despise’. The commentators draw three senses from it: aversion or disgust (Śaṅkara), censure (Deśika) and, keeping the root’s sense of guarding, the wish to protect oneself from fear (Madhva’s cited verse: «यः पश्येत् स भयाभावान्नात्मानं गोप्तुमिच्छति»). The Mādhyandina recension reads a different verb, vi cikitsati, ‘doubts’, and Mahīdhara explains: «आत्मनोऽन्यत्पश्यतः सर्वः संदेहो भवत्यात्मानमेवात्यन्तं शुद्धं निरन्तरं पश्यतो न संदेहावकाश इति भावः» — all doubt arises in one who sees something other than the self. The two recensions end the same thought differently: freedom from aversion, or freedom from doubt.

commentary.q: What is the relation of the self to Brahman here?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The mantra does not use the word brahman. Śaṅkara’s reading makes ‘the self’ of the seer and ‘the self in all beings’ one and the same, so the verse becomes a statement of non-duality. Deśika and Madhva distinguish the seer’s self from the Self that indwells all beings; for them the verse describes seeing the Lord everywhere, and everything as resting in him. The grammar — one word ātman in both phrases — allows either; the decision is made by the rest of each commentator’s system.

advaita.text: The self seen in all beings is the seer’s own self, pure consciousness without qualities: «अहं सर्वप्रत्ययसाक्षिभूतश्चेतयिता केवलो निर्गुणोऽनेनैव स्वरूपेणाव्यक्तादीनां स्थावरान्तानामहमेवात्मेति». Aversion presupposes something other than the self; where nothing else is seen, it cannot arise.

visistadvaita.text: The self here is the inner self of all, the Lord («सर्वान्तरात्मविषयः»); all beings rest in him and he pervades them. Seeing everything as having Brahman for its self, the knower finds nothing to censure, as one does not censure one’s own glory («स्वात्मविभूतिन्यायात्»).

dvaita.text: Madhva comments only with a verse he cites as śruti of Saukarāyaṇa: the one who sees the all-pervading Paramātman, and all in the Paramātman, has no fear and so does not wish to guard himself («सर्वगं परमात्मानं सर्वं च परमात्मनि । यः पश्येत् स भयाभावान्नात्मानं गोप्तुमिच्छति»). The seer and the Paramātman remain distinct. The verse is reported as cited by Madhva; its source has not been verified.

schools.disagreement: All three agree that the knower sees the self in all and all in the self, and that a negative state ends. They disagree on whose self it is — the seer’s own, identical with all (Śaṅkara), or the Lord as the inner self of all (Deśika, Madhva) — and on what ends: aversion (Śaṅkara), censure (Deśika) or the fear that makes one guard oneself (Madhva).

parallels.note: The same closing words, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: ‘when one sees this self as God, the lord of what was and what will be, one does not shrink from him’. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka belongs to the same Śukla Yajurveda tradition.
The Kaṭha repeats the same half-verse as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, of one who knows the self ‘close at hand’.

The Gītā’s yogin ‘sees the self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the self’ — the two directions of Īśā 6, in the same order reversed, close enough in wording to be a conscious echo, though no commentator here says so.

parallels.quote: यो मां पश्यति सर्वत्र सर्वं च मयि पश्यति
parallels.note: The next Gītā verse puts the same vision in the first person of the Lord: ‘who sees me everywhere and everything in me’. It supports the theistic reading as the Gītā’s own development of the idea.
‘The supreme Lord standing equally in all beings’: the seeing that removes partiality.

contemporary.text: Leaders are often taught to ‘manage stakeholders’ — a phrase that already places others outside oneself, to be handled. Contempt in organisations usually begins as distance: the department that does not understand us, the customers who complain, the people a decision affects but who are not in the room. The mantra’s vision runs the other way: it begins with seeing oneself in others, and only then describes the result, that aversion falls away. A leader need not hold any metaphysical view to notice that decisions made from contempt and decisions made from a sense of shared stake tend to differ. This is a reflection on the teaching, not part of it.

reflect.beginner: Think of someone you find hard to like. Can you name one thing in them that is also in you?
reflect.deeper: If aversion needs an ‘other’, is the self that the mantra speaks of something I have, or something I am, and does it leave room for anyone to be other?
reflect.practice: On a walk or a commute, silently say ‘in me’ for three people you pass, and ‘in them’ for yourself. Afterwards, note whether you noticed them differently.

references.text: The pada-pāṭha of VS 40.6 divides «आ॒त्मन्। ए॒व।» and «न। वि। चि॒कि॒त्स॒ति॒», confirming both the Saṃhitā locative ātman and the Mādhyandina verb.

flags.note: Kāṇva ‘na vijugupsate’ against Mādhyandina ‘na vi cikitsati’ (VS 40.6): a recensional difference, recorded in corrections.json; the edition follows the Kāṇva.
